newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Nordbanken sees more sector restructuring.
newsitem.headline: Nordbanken sees more sector restructuring.

text.p: Swedish state-controlled bank Nordbanken said on Friday it expected a continued sector restructuring aimed at boosting shareholder value and broadening the customer base.
Nordbanken's chief executive Hans Dalborg told Reuters in an interview that the bank did not need a larger branch network and had no intention of letting go of its asset management.

Dalborg's statement appeared to squash rumours that Nordbanken may buy rival S-E-Banken's office network while S-E-Banken would take Nordbanken's asset management. "Nordbanken's target is to increase shareholder value through a continuous profit growth," Dalborg said.

"This you can reach by becoming better at what you already do. Then our mission is also to be aware of and create structural deals. The structural solutions don't have to mean more offices but a broader customer base."
"We won't let go of asset management. Period. That is an integrated part of the bank's product range," he said.
Dalborg expected a continued restructuring of the Swedish banking sector but refrained from guessing about how the market will look in a few years time.
The sector has already seen upheaval with two large deals struck in the past year and numerous small stakes grabbed.
Handelsbanken bought mortgage lender Stadshypotek for 22.9 billion crowns ($2.9 billion) and Swedbank merged with Foreningsbanken, forming ForeningsSparbanken.
Earlier this week, Swedbank gobbled up a piece of newcomer HSB Bank and in June it announced it was about to acquire 7.4 percent of shares in Estonian bank Hoiupank.
The deals come ahead of Europe's economic and monetary union (EMU) as banks fear they will meet tougher international competition from January 1, 1999.
In addition, mergers will save some information technology costs as the banks have to update their electronic systems ahead of both EMU and the turn of the century.
But the most talked-about merger is the expected marriage of S-E-Banken and Nordbanken which failed in the spring.

Analysts still expect the two to become one this year as the government's 1997 budget includes sales revenues from its 59.4 percent Nordbanken stake and the ruling Social Democrats need money to woo voters ahead of September 1998 elections.
